synopsis: Driver-/operator-in-the-loop testing puts a real person in a simulator to study reactions to warnings, delays and braking; it assesses the human response rather than sensor detection or real braking hardware [f13402, f571, f578]. The booklet’s strongest off-road human-interface evidence is ACARP’s modified haul-truck simulator research in Australian open-cut coal operations during 2017–2019: a richer schematic proximity display reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time, although benefits were smaller in an experiment with fewer experienced drivers [f3465, f3468, f3466, f3467]. That research addressed proximity advisory rather than automatic braking, and no off-road study of operators experiencing automatic braking in a simulator was found [f573, f576]. Simulator-to-field transfer remains unestablished for demanding operating conditions, and simulator studies cannot establish months-long complacency, risk compensation or production-pressure effects; operational monitoring and field time remain necessary [f3469, f580, f792, f767]. On-road findings also resist simple assumptions: a 2025 simulator study reported no cry-wolf effect at 33% false alarms but did report unnecessary braking, while other on-road truck warning data showed a strong cry-wolf effect [f3335, f3336, f3623]. The program therefore recommends operator studies before prototype safety testing and potentially requires human-in-the-loop evidence for operator-dependent safety claims, but the setup duration for operator-simulator capability is undocumented [f13415, f11833, f849].
